detail: supported

Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which composites opacities, this method sums projected 2D densities, fundamentally addressing integration bias issues where learning integrated density in 2D leads to inconsistencies in 3D density retrieval [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the method renders X-ray projections by integrating 3D Gaussians along ray paths, resulting in a sum of 2D Gaussians (Eq. 7 and surrounding text), rather than alpha-compositing. It further explains that standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learns an integrated density in the 2D image plane, which leads to 'integration bias' and 'inconsistency in density retrieval' because different views yield different results for the same 3D density. The proposed method addresses this by assigning the actual 3D density to the kernel and computing the 2D projection forward, thus solving the issue.

The evidence explicitly states in the 'Integration bias' section of Source [S1] that the method scales the density with a factor $ eta_i$ (denoted as $mu_i$ in the claim, likely a typo for $mu_i$ or $ eta_i$ which represents the scaling factor) defined as $ eta_i = (2pi| etilde{Sigma}_i|/| at{Sigma}_i|)^{1/2}$. Specifically, it says: 'we scale the density with a covariance-related factor $ eta_i = (2pi| etilde{Sigma}_i|/| at{Sigma}_i|)^{1/2} :  at{rho}_i =  eta_i rho_i$'. This confirms that the projected density $ at{rho}_i$ is obtained by scaling the original density $rho_i$ with the factor $ eta_i$ (referred to as $mu_i$ in the claim).

Integrate the 3D Gaussian along the ray path (z-axis in ray space) [S1].

The claim states that the method involves integrating 3D Gaussians along the ray path (z-axis in ray space). The evidence explicitly supports this in multiple places: 1) The source notes state 'Rendering X-ray projections by integrating 3D Gaussians along ray paths'. 2) The mathematical formulation in the source passages shows $I_r(r) = M Z X G3i (r(t)|ρi , pi , Σi )dt$, indicating integration along the ray. 3) The text explains that Gaussians are transferred to 'ray space' where 'viewing rays are parallel to the third coordinate axis', facilitating analytical integration. 4) The result of this integration is described as summing 2D Gaussians. All facts in the claim are present and supported by the evidence.

The new position in ray space is $\tilde{p}_i = \phi(p_i)$ [S1].

The claim states that the new position in ray space is defined as $p̃_i = φ(p_i)$. Source [S1] explicitly defines this relationship in multiple places: 1) In the notes, it states 'p̃_i = T * p_i (implied by 'transfer')' but later clarifies in the Appendix section that 'p̃_i = ϕ(p)' (Eq. 11). 2) In the main text under 'Transformation', it says 'p̃_i ∈ R^3 is the new Gaussian position obtained through projective mapping ϕ'. 3) In the Appendix (Eq. 11), it explicitly writes 'p̃_i = ϕ(p)'. The symbol φ in the claim corresponds to ϕ in the text. Thus, the evidence fully supports the claim.

Render the projection by summing the contributions of all 2D Gaussians [S1].

The notes also confirm this by stating the result is 'a sum of 2D Gaussians rather than alpha-compositing'.
